newsitem.title: USA: GM Canada strike effect widens in U.S..
newsitem.headline: GM Canada strike effect widens in U.S..

text.p: The shockwaves from the strike against General Motors Corp. in Canada widened Monday as the automaker said the walkout has forced it to idle more than 5,900 workers in the United States and Mexico.

GM said 1,350 second-shift workers at its Cadillac luxury car assembly plant in Detroit did not report to work Monday, and an additional 850 workers were laid off at the automaker's Ypsilanti, Mich., transmission plant.
The Cadillac plant, which employs about 3,000 hourly workers, is expected to be completely shut down by the end of the first shift on Tuesday. It builds Seville, DeVille and Eldorado models.

GM's Delphi Automotive Systems division said it had idled 1,661 parts workers at plants in Michigan, Ohio and Mexico and an additional 50 workers were laid off at a powertrain components plant in Flint, Mich.
Another 2,000 idle workers at engine and transmission plants were forced to stay off the job on the 12th day of the strike in Canada.

GM's 26,000 Canadian Auto Workers union members launched an escalating strike on Oct. 3 that shut down all of GM's Canadian production on Oct. 9. Contract talks between GM and the union remained deadlocked over the issue of GM's ability to shift work to lower-cost outside suppliers, known as outsourcing.
The CAW wants tough restrictions on the practice to protect jobs, while GM says it needs flexibility in parts purchases if it wants to become competitive.
CAW President Buzz Hargrove said talks were dormant on Monday as Canada celebrated its national Thanksgiving Day holiday.
"I talked to the company's chief negotiator on the phone today, but he said he didn't have anything for me," Hargrove said. "There's a lot of good debate, but very little progress."
He said GM appears to have dug in for a long strike, but added that the union's resolve to protect jobs remained strong.
Hargrove said CAW members were fully behind the walkout and were willing to assume some hardship. "This is not Buzz Hargrove's strike. It's a rank-and-file strike," he said.

Analysts said a prolonged strike in Canada will eventually force the automaker to halt most of its U.S. production. As assembly plants shut down, the plants that supply them also will be forced to lay off workers.
Independent parts suppliers -- the firms that GM wants to buy more components from -- also continued to worry about the effects the strike will have on their financial performance.
Federal Screw Works, a Detroit-based maker of automotive fasterners, said a prolonged strike against GM Canada "will adversely affect our business."

Competitors, however, do not anticipate a big windfall from the GM strike. Chrysler Corp. Chief Financial Officer Gary Valade said he believed GM dealers have sufficient inventories to last them for several weeks in most vehicle segments.

According to Automotive News, GM dealers had a 69-day supply of cars and trucks as of Oct. 1, including a 78-day supply of trucks and a 62-day supply of cars. Automakers normally consider a 60-day supply of vehicles to be ideal.
Vehicles with the smallest inventories include Saturn cars, with a 37-day supply, and GMC Yukon full-size sport/utility vehicles, also at 37 days.

GM vehicles with more than 100 days of inventory include Chevrolet and GMC full- vans and mid-size vans; the Chevrolet Camaro and Pontiac Firebird sport coupes; Geo Tracker sport/utility vehicles; Oldsmobile Silhouette and Pontiac Trans Sport minivans; and GMC Sonoma compact pickup trucks.
